 House District 14
 



Ava Flanell (incumbent)
Age: 39
City of residence: Colorado Springs
Occupation: Business owner and state representative
 


 



Troy Vanderhule
Age: 55
City of residence: Colorado Springs
Occupation: Marketing executive
 


Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district?: 
FLANELL: I’d start by taking my friend on a scenic drive through Garden of the Gods, one of Colorado’s most iconic landmarks known for its towering red rock formations, stunning mountain views, and unforgettable scenery. After taking in the natural beauty of the park, I’d head to Glen Eyrie Castle for afternoon tea. Built in the late 1800s by Colorado Springs founder William Jackson Palmer, the historic English Tudor-style castle offers a peaceful and elegant experience nestled among the foothills and rock formations of Colorado Springs.
VANDERHULE: Part of House District 14 goes right down the access points of Garden of the Gods and the Glen Eyrie Castle. Both are great places to visit for out-of-town guests.
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address them? 
FLANELL: Constituents in House District 14 consistently point to affordability as the most pressing issue facing their families. Rising housing costs, increasing energy prices, and the growing burden of regulations and fees on businesses are all contributing factors, and those costs are often passed on to consumers. To address these challenges, I support reforming Colorado’s construction defect laws to include a right-to-remedy process that encourages the development of more attainable housing while still protecting homeowners. We need policies that make it easier to build entry-level homes and expand housing opportunities for working families. On energy, I oppose mandates that drive up utility costs faster than our infrastructure can reliably support. I also believe we should avoid shutting down reliable energy sources prematurely and ensure decisions are based on cost, reliability, and capacity. Expanding consumer choice will allow homeowners to select the most practical and affordable energy options for their needs. For small businesses, we need a serious review of state mandates and operating costs, including the long-term impact of the FAMLI program, as well as excessive licensing requirements, regulatory burdens, and fees. Reducing these pressures will help businesses grow, create jobs, and keep costs lower for consumers.
VANDERHULE: Colorado has a runaway cost-of-living problem. We rank as one of the worst states for violent crime and overall crime. We strangle businesses and prosperity through radical social ideologies and business regulations. These are major issues for all Coloradans. For House District 14 specifically, housing and public schools are significant issues as well. There is not enough housing available and housing costs are too high. This means there are not enough young families moving into our communities. Our public schools are experiencing declining enrollment. More students are opting for charter schools and homeschools. The first solution to these problems is allowing more houses to be built. We need to reduce the burdensome regulations on housing and home building. The second solution is to fix Colorado public schools. We need school choice, but we also need successful public schools. Put the focus back on learning. Allow school discipline that would remove disruptive students. Reward good teachers. Remove poorly performing teachers. We need to make public schools a viable option.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation? 

FLANELL: The state is facing a significant budget challenge after relying on one-time federal COVID funds to support ongoing programs that should have been time-limited or structured with clear sunset provisions. At the same time, Medicaid enrollment and costs have grown faster than projected, making it essential to strengthen oversight and ensure taxpayer dollars are being used efficiently and appropriately. To address this, we need a more robust audit and accountability process that regularly evaluates program performance using clear, measurable outcomes. When programs are found to be ineffective, duplicative, or wasteful, the state should have the discipline to reform or eliminate them rather than continue automatic funding. This includes reviewing existing programs that expanded during the COVID era and determining which should be scaled back or discontinued. We should also strengthen eligibility verification and safeguards across public assistance programs to ensure benefits are directed to individuals who are legally eligible, while protecting resources for those who truly need them. Combined with targeted audits to identify fraud, waste, and abuse, this approach would improve accountability and help stabilize the budget without compromising core services.
VANDERHULE: First, Colorado has enough revenue to meet its budgetary needs. But the problem is the one-party rule of radical Democrats who are spending on social experiments and social priorities. Our Colorado Democrats are not limiting funding for state-funded abortions, trans surgeries, and illegal aliens. But this radical Legislature is willing to cut vital funding for services that go to Colorado citizens and communities. Second, fraud, waste, and abuse need to be excised from the Colorado budget. Huge amounts of funding go to nonprofits and service providers in Colorado. There needs to be active auditing and transparency about where this funding goes. Third, Colorado actively strangles local businesses. Colorado is one of the most heavily regulated states in the U.S. If you have a business, Colorado imposes radical social policies on your operations and Colorado will take more and more of your profits every year. For Colorado to return to a positive budget, we need to stop unlimited funding for radical social ideologies, we need to protect Colorado cities and families, and we need to allow Colorado businesses to thrive. When Colorado was a red state, we had all of those things: safety, security, and prosperity.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers? 
FLANELL: I’d like to continue learning more about data centers and their long-term impacts before taking a firm position, but I do believe there should be reasonable safeguards in place as these facilities expand. First, local communities should have a strong voice in zoning and siting decisions to ensure nearby residents and infrastructure are not negatively impacted. Second, the financial burden of large-scale development should not be shifted onto taxpayers through increased utility or infrastructure costs. I also believe Colorado must be mindful of natural resource use, especially water and energy consumption. Wherever possible, data centers should prioritize alternative cooling methods or the use of reclaimed water instead of potable water. Facilities should also have contingency plans in place to address periods of water scarcity and increased energy demand.
VANDERHULE: I support American innovation and technological leadership, but not on the backs of Colorado families and taxpayers. Data centers are welcome if they follow the rules, respect local communities, cover their true costs, and strengthen our energy independence and way of life. I would think about policies in this order: Local control first: zoning, land use, and permitting decisions belong to cities, counties, and homeowners, not state or federal mandates. We need to defend property rights and oppose top-down imposition on rural or suburban neighborhoods. No taxpayer subsidies or corporate welfare: Data centers should not receive special tax breaks, grants, or ratepayer-funded infrastructure upgrades. They must pay for their electricity, water, roads, and grid upgrades. Energy abundance over rationing: I would argue that America needs more power. This includes nuclear, natural gas, and coal. Taxpayers should not have to subsidize the massive consumption of data centers. Data centers should not drive up residential electricity bills or strain water resources in arid states like Colorado. 
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy? 
FLANELL: Working across the aisle is essential, especially in a Legislature where Republicans hold just 35 of 100 seats. In that environment, meaningful progress requires finding common ground on policies that genuinely improve the lives of Coloradans and have a realistic path to becoming law. I believe lasting solutions require communication and collaboration, both across party lines and within my own party. I’m willing to work with any legislator who is serious about lowering costs, strengthening communities, protecting constitutional rights, and improving the quality of life for Colorado families. I won’t support policies that expand government overreach or undermine individual freedoms. I evaluate legislation based on its real-world impact on affordability, public safety, economic opportunity, and the rights of Colorado citizens, not simply on partisan labels.
VANDERHULE: Returning political power to the people of Colorado is the main role of a Colorado legislator. Insisting on the rights and freedom of the people of Colorado is the main role of a Colorado legislator. Legislators represent the people. Therefore, the only goal of legislation should be to ensure that the people of Colorado are keeping their rights, their freedoms, their businesses, and their right to self defense. Working across the aisle is great, but only if we are finding ways to allow businesses to prosper, communities to flourish, and people to be safe. Most of the legislation over the last decade of radical one-party rule has strangled our businesses, impoverished our cities, endangered our citizens, stolen our TABOR, and emburdened us with massive debt. Coloradans do not want more legislators who are going to compromise away more of their freedoms, rights, and money. Compromise and concession can only be reached if we are finding the ways Coloradans can prosper and flourish.
What is one bill, vote or other legislative action you’ve taken that you feel best demonstrates your qualification for reelection?
FLANELL: This year, I spent much of my time in a defensive posture, working to stop or improve legislation that would have negatively impacted Colorado families and businesses. In just four months, the legislature considered more than 600 bills, reflecting both the volume and complexity of policymaking in our state. At the end of the session, it was brought to my attention that I was among the top legislators that defeated the most bills. In a state that ranks among the most regulated in the country, I consider that a meaningful accomplishment, especially given that committees like Judiciary have, at times, advanced some of the most concerning legislation in recent years. This required significant behind-the-scenes work, strategic coordination, and long hours that most people never saw. In the end, I believe it was beneficial for my constituents and for Colorado.
Are there any votes the incumbent has taken in the Legislature you disagree with? What are they and why would you have voted differently?
VANDERHULE: There are specific votes the incumbent has cast that I would disagree with. But the larger issue is that, fundamentally, the House District 14 incumbent has a differing standpoint on governing and policymaking. There is a current group of Republican legislators who believe their role is to compromise with the radical Democrats and their radical policies. These Republicans will tell you they have to compromise away your freedoms and rights because they are the minority party in the Legislature. These Republicans will tell you they have to compromise away your freedoms and rights because that will hopefully attract some of Colorado’s unaffiliated voters. There is a group of Republican legislators who enjoy being courted by lobbyists and having their favor curried by special interests. These are the same Republicans who will tell you they have no choice but to compromise away your rights and freedoms. I believe the role of a Colorado representative is to ensure the rights and freedoms of every Coloradan. There cannot be compromise with proposals, bills, or legislators who want to weaken Colorado citizens.

Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district? 
KOCH: One place I’d love to take an out-of-town friend in House District 16 is Pulpit Rock. Pulpit Rock gives you some of the best panoramic views of Colorado Springs and Pikes Peak, and it’s a great way to experience the natural beauty that makes this community so special. Pulpit Rock is peaceful and allows one to take in the beautiful views while avoiding large crowds and the noise of the typical tourist spots. Pulpit Rock was the first hike I did when I moved to Colorado Springs in 2007 and it left a lasting impression on me.  
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
KOCH: Residents throughout House District 16 tell me that affordability is one of their biggest concerns. Families are feeling the pressure of rising costs everywhere. People are working hard but still feel like it’s becoming more difficult to get ahead or even maintain the quality of life they once had here in House District 16. Government should focus on creating an environment where families can thrive, not make life more expensive. I will work to support fiscally responsible policies that help lower the tax burden on working families and reduce unnecessary government regulations that drive up costs. I will advocate for small businesses that are already struggling with overregulation. Colorado needs leadership that prioritizes responsible budgeting, public safety, economic opportunity, and policies that make Colorado more affordable for the next generation. People want practical solutions and accountable leadership. 
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation?
KOCH: Balancing the budget starts with the government getting back to basics and cutting spending that doesn’t directly help everyday Coloradans. People notice when the state spends $3 million renovating the governor’s office while families are struggling with groceries, housing, utility bills and other everyday costs. We need to take a serious look at administrative growth, consultant contracts, duplicative programs, taxpayer-funded lobbying and projects that sound good but don’t produce measurable results. Colorado’s recent budget shortfall of roughly $1 to $1.5 billion was eye-opening. Families expect the state government to show the same financial discipline they’ve had to show at home. Government should focus first on core responsibilities like public safety, roads, water, infrastructure, and education instead of constantly growing bureaucracy and long-term spending commitments.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers?
KOCH: While data centers can bring jobs and economic growth, they place major demands on electricity, water, land use, and infrastructure. Some large data centers use as much electricity as a small city and can use millions of gallons of water each year for cooling systems. That’s a major concern for Colorado, especially considering that water resources are already limited and many communities are worried about long-term water availability and drought conditions. Communities should not be forced to absorb those impacts without a voice in the process. Residents deserve transparency about how proposed projects could affect energy demand, utility costs, water usage, traffic, emergency services and the character of their neighborhoods before approvals are granted. The state should be cautious about offering large taxpayer-funded incentives without clear long-term benefits for local communities. If companies receive public support, there should be accountability and protections to ensure residents are not left paying higher infrastructure or utility costs later. Colorado should remain open to innovation and economic development, but growth needs to be responsible and sustainable. We have to make sure we are protecting our natural resources and quality of life. 
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy?
KOCH: Elected officials should be respectful and willing to work with anyone when it benefits the people of Colorado; however, I don’t believe compromise for the sake of compromise is the answer. Decades of bipartisan deals and constant expansion of government are part of what has made life more complicated and expensive. These deals have made living in Colorado more difficult for Colorado families. Government was instituted to protect our God-given rights and uphold the Constitution, not to continuously grow and overregulate. We need leaders who are willing to reexamine existing policies and roll back unnecessary government overreach. We need leaders who are willing to get back to the core responsibilities the government was meant to fulfill. That doesn’t mean refusing to work with others. If there are good ideas that genuinely help Coloradans, I’m willing to have those conversations with anyone, but my focus will always be on principles, protecting individual liberty, and making government more accountable to the people, not finding middle ground to pass more legislation.

What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
RUMFELT: The biggest issue I hear about from residents is the cost of housing. There is no single cause, which means there will not be a single solution. State and local governments, builders, developers, and community leaders all need to work together to address affordability. One major factor is the growing cost of regulations and building requirements. This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation?

Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district? 
ALEXANDER: There is so much to see and do in House District 60. However, some of them do stand out like: The Royal Gorge Bridge, several 14ers, and Pikes Peak. With that said, we are also home to some of the greatest fishing, camping, hiking and hunting anywhere in the world. What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
 ALEXANDER: We are subject to a myriad of challenges here in House District 60. To name a few, government overreach and complex unfunded mandates and regulations, water rights issues, ever-growing urban development at the cost of rural Coloradans, the state constantly inventing new taxes under the guise of “fees,” the violation of our Second Amendment rights, the unaffordable home market, high crime, drugs, homelessness. The list could go on. Simply put, Colorado is one of the most poorly managed states in the United States and is also one of the worst places to run a small business. There is much work to be done.  So why stay and fight? As a fourth generation Colorado native, this is my family’s home and has been for more than 130 years. I am fighting to take back Colorado so that our future generations will have a wonderful place to call home.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation?
ALEXANDER: Medicaid is a bloated money vacuum; cuts there alone would balance the budget. There are many other places, too. The first thing we need to do is make sure that Medicaid recipients are legal citizens and that they are employed or seeking employment. We also need to look into the state-funded non-citizen health programs. We must make sure that Medicaid is helping those that are in dire need and not just used as a permanent subsidy for those who are able-bodied and capable of work. In a decade Medicaid has surpassed K-12 education in the budget, not by a little, but by a huge margin. We do not have a lack of tax revenue; we have a spending problem. We must learn how to say no to bad spending.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers?
ALEXANDER: I would say that any policies that we implement as a state should be one of responsible growth. We want investment and job growth for Colorado, especially in the world of ever-expanding AI. With that said, I realize the issue of energy and water usage. We must ask Big Tech to carry that burden and not expect Colorado families to carry that burden. We can still make Colorado a tech leader without losing our rural identity. I would love to see rural Colorado have the opportunity to grow and have jobs in this market, as well. We should encourage growth there and not just cram everything into Denver.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy?
ALEXANDER: My view is simple: Values are for holding, and policy is for winning. I am not going to the Capitol to be part of the “go-along-to-get-along” club. We’ve seen where that gets us.  Colorado is the home to record debt and government overreach. I have no interest in compromising my morals or my conservative convictions to please people whose policies and beliefs are broken. However, in my time on the Cañon City School Board I learned that you can be the most steadfast person in the room and still be effective. I will work with anyone; Republican, Democrat, or Independent, but we must protect our water, defend our Second Amendment, and stop the state from overspending. Let’s be clear: I’m there to advance the values of rural Colorado and House District 60, not to benefit Denver bureaucrats.

text:
A view of the Colorado Capitol on Jan. 25, 2024. (Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)Coloradans will vote in primary elections June 30 to determine which candidates will represent their party in the general election in November.

The elections cover Colorado’s four statewide constitutional offices, one U.S. Senate seat, all eight of the state’s congressional districts, state legislative districts and other races. Colorado Newsline sent questionnaires to candidates in contested primary races and is publishing responses as part of its voter guide to help Coloradans make informed choices.
Ballots were scheduled to be mailed to all registered voters in Colorado starting June 8.
Voters can contact their county clerk if they have not received their ballot or check the online BallotTrax system. They can also visit the secretary of state’s website to make a plan to vote in person ahead of or on Election Day. Ballots need to be received by the county clerk by 7 p.m. on that day, so voters should mail their ballot at least eight days ahead of time or drop it off in person.
Use the Colorado General Assembly’s Find My Legislator tool to determine what House and Senate districts you live in.
Candidates often refer to the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights as TABOR. That is a constitutional amendment that limits state spending according to population and inflation growth. Everything over that cap must be returned to taxpayers via a variety of refund mechanisms outlined in state statute. TABOR also requires voter approval for new taxes.

 House District 5
 



Justine Sandoval
Age: 40
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: Grassroots organizer
 


 


Sterling Simms
Age: 25
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: Senior Outreach Manager, Office of Mayor Mike Johnston
 


Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district? 
SANDOVAL: As a person who has grown up in Denver my entire life, this is a question I get a lot. People often ask me where to go and how to really experience Denver, and I take a lot of pride in being kind of an unofficial ambassador for my city. Depending on the season, I’d probably take them to a Rockies game at Coors Field. They may not win, but there’s not a bad seat in the stadium. You get a 360 view of the game, an amazing look at the downtown skyline, and views of the mountains usually paired with one of those world-famous Colorado sunsets. I’d also take them down to the Santa Fe Arts District. We could grab a coffee at Tonantzin Casa de Café or get a bite to eat somewhere along Santa Fe while walking around La Alma–Lincoln Park, one of Denver’s oldest neighborhoods and the city’s first historic cultural district honoring the Chicano Movement. The neighborhood is full of incredible murals and local art connected to the Chicano Mural Movement, and it tells an important story about the culture and community that helped shape Denver. 
SIMMS: Downtown Denver has experienced significant change since the pandemic (and) it’s important to celebrate how far we’ve come, from reopening 16th street, to reactivating our beloved downtown public spaces and bringing our unhoused neighbors indoors. I would, and have, taken my out of town friends to the heart of Downtown Denver to see a show, enjoy a drink or a meal on 16th street, or to see a show at one of our amazing venues. Soon to be home to every Denver sports team, House District 5 has so much to offer!
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
SANDOVAL: One of the biggest issues I hear from residents is a little more abstract than the usual policy conversations about housing, affordability, or public safety. People feel increasingly disconnected from each other and from the neighborhoods they call home. Our district includes the heart of Denver and some of the city’s most historic communities, and people want to make sure that as Denver grows, we don’t lose the sense of community that makes these neighborhoods special. As a state House candidate, I want to help unite our district by investing in the things that bring people together. That means improving public transit and accessibility so our neighborhoods are better connected and easier for everyone to navigate. It means supporting small businesses, especially local restaurants and neighborhood storefronts that serve as gathering places but are struggling with rising costs and rent.  This district needs more diverse and attainable housing options so longtime residents, young families, workers, artists, and newcomers alike can afford to live and build community here. Denver should continue to grow, but in a way that keeps our neighborhoods welcoming, connected, and accessible to people from all backgrounds. 
SIMMS: When talking to my neighbors in House District 5, the challenges they raise are often the same. Many are struggling to keep up with the rising costs of housing, many are heartbroken by the scenes of addiction and mental illness that is plaguing so many in our community, they’re worried about the safety of their streets, and the quality of the air they breathe and the water they drink. These are all symptoms of our deeply entrenched crisis of inequality. I want to address these crises by addressing the root causes, not simply the symptoms. I want to leverage a public bank to provide the cheapest access to capital for housing development across the entire housing spectrum, bringing units online to reduce the costs of housing across the board. I want to invest in services across the entire spectrum of recovery. You need to meet our most vulnerable residents where they are, and when the services they rely on don’t exist, they have no choice but to get left behind. And finally, I want to divest our tax dollars from extractive industry which continues to pollute our communities in pursuit of private profits.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation?
SANDOVAL: Colorado’s budget situation is honestly exhausting to watch because every year we end up having the same conversation about cutting services people depend on the most. Our schools are comically underfunded, healthcare costs are through the roof, and communities need more support, but TABOR keeps the state stuck with one hand tied behind its back. I don’t think the answer is cutting programs that help working families, kids, seniors, people with disabilities, or people struggling to get by. I support getting rid of TABOR and updating Colorado’s outdated tax code, including moving toward a graduated income tax so the wealthiest people pay more instead of putting all the financial pressure on everyday Coloradans. I support legislation that would help Colorado actually invest in public education, healthcare, disability services, housing, and transportation instead of constantly fighting over scraps. Colorado is a wealthy state. We should be able to fund good schools, accessible communities, functioning transit, and basic services without acting like that’s unrealistic. People are tired of hearing there’s never enough money while costs keep rising and communities keep being asked to settle for less.
SIMMS: We have to be clear-eyed about the fact that further cuts in state spending will continue to diminish the quality of human services that our neighbors rely on every day. The solution to our budget crisis requires more than cutting spending, and raising revenue continues to be a challenge under TABOR. We need to become the second state in the nation to charter a public bank off of North Dakota’s model to maximize the impact of the tax revenue we already collect. Simply by diverting our tax dollars out of Wall Street, institutions will provide the revenue stream we need not only to fix our structural deficit, but to generate excess revenue which can be returned to the state’s general fund in the form of a dividend.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers?
SANDOVAL: Data centers, especially in Denver, have become one of the biggest topics of concern across the nation right now because people feel like these projects are being forced into neighborhoods with zero transparency, zero regard for the long-term impact on the community, and almost no real public input. I believe the state should enact much stronger policies around where data centers can be built, how much water and energy they are allowed to use, and whether communities actually want them there in the first place. That includes stricter environmental review standards, limits on water consumption, protections against building these facilities near residential neighborhoods, and giving local communities real power to reject projects that do not align with their needs. Colorado is already dealing with water scarcity, rising energy demands, and the realities of climate change. Water should be for people, agriculture, and life first, not machines. I am not against technology or economic growth, but I do not think corporations should be able to come into our communities, drain resources, and reshape neighborhoods without accountability.
SIMMS: We need to understand that data centers will be needed for our own domestic use of AI. The concerns held by community are very real. They’re scared about their water being contaminated, their energy costs rising and environmentally sensitive spaces being contaminated further. I think we need to pass legislation as a state that ensures our data centers aren’t adding onto the negative impacts communities already face from industry. We need to ensure that our data centers conform to the highest standards of environmental responsibility, and we must protect rate payers from increases in energy and water use rate hikes.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy?
SANDOVAL: I think people are tired of elected officials treating politics like a performance instead of focusing on solving problems. I’m going to the Capitol to fight for the people and values I believe in, but I also understand that meaningful change only happens when people are willing to work together. I come from an activist background, and for a long time my role was pushing people in power to act from outside the Capitol. Now, if I want to pass meaningful policy, I have to navigate a Legislature made up of 64 other representatives with different perspectives and priorities. That means fighting hard for what I believe in while also being willing to build relationships and find common ground where possible. I’ll work with anyone who comes to the table in good faith and is serious about finding real solutions for Colorado. I also think collaboration within the Democratic Party is really important right now. I want to come in with a clean slate, work with as many people as possible, and be an effective and collaborative member of the State House.
SIMMS: Three years in city government taught me that the government can’t do anything alone — the job is to be a convening power. I’ve built coalitions with business owners, nonprofits, mutual aid volunteers, and service providers because they have capacity government doesn’t, and I’ll legislate the same way: judge every partner by whether they help the people we serve, not by their label. Good policy is measured by its impact on the ground, and I’ll work with whoever is serious about that.
House District 6
 



Sean Camacho (incumbent)
Age: 43
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: Attorney, state representative
 


 


Iris Halpern
Age: 45
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: Civil rights attorney
 


Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district?
CAMACHO: One of the greatest things about House District 6 is that it is in the heart of Denver and includes some of the best businesses, attractions, and public spaces in the state. One of my favorite locations in my district is the Denver Botanic Gardens. My family visits the Botanic Gardens multiple times a year, and it is the first thing that comes to mind when I think about what I would show an out-of-town visitor. It not only holds great events and exhibits year-round but also represents Colorado’s commitment to and appreciation of nature.
HALPERN: That’s a tough one, we have a lot of great places to visit including the Capitol in my district, but I would probably take an out-of-town friend to the Botanic Gardens and Cheesman Park.
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
CAMACHO: I frequently check in with my constituents to gauge their top issues, and it is repeatedly clear that my constituents care deeply about a broad range of issues, from affordability and the high cost of living to health care access and support. One of the most consistent issues that my constituents prioritize is TABOR’s impact on our state finances. I am considered one of the foremost experts on TABOR in Colorado, having worked on the TABOR lawsuit early in my legal career and being the first legislator to introduce legislation challenging TABOR’s constitutionality. As we cut nearly $1 billion from our state budget each year due to TABOR and H.R. 1, the conversation around TABOR has intensified significantly. Another top priority is standing up against the Trump administration’s dangerous agenda, which has specifically targeted Colorado. This includes protecting SNAP, gender-affirming care, immigration and civil rights. During my first term, I effectively represented my district’s priorities in my votes and the bills I ran, as well as stood up to Trump and special interests that want to derail Colorado’s future.
HALPERN: In my district, residents’ concerns run the gamut. Some frequently raised issues include affordability, specifically affordable housing, repealing TABOR so we can secure more support for education, healthcare, and housing, and implement a more progressive taxation system, regulation of artificial intelligence, and strong resident concern for immigrant and constitutional rights.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation?
CAMACHO: Having cut over $3 billion from our budget, we are long past the point of trimming the excess or finding spare change in our couch cushions. We have to make deeply painful cuts that will dramatically impact the lives of Coloradans who need help across the state. In my view, all roads lead back to TABOR. If we don’t finally rid Colorado of TABOR, we will continue to have to cut crucial services that my constituents rely on, especially in health care. As the General Assembly’s leading voice against TABOR, my top priority is to dismantle this broken budget structure so we can restore and expand funding for important state services, and I am the legislator with the experience to make this happen.
HALPERN: We can always look for redundant spending or areas where we can be more efficient or reduce fraud, but the truth is that cutting essential services and programs cannot be a problem we face every year. We need to repeal TABOR and implement a progressive taxation system on wealthy individuals and corporations. We need the capability to raise revenue to adequately fund services and programs. For example, right now, Colorado ranks 48th in the country for public school funding. We are paying about $2,400 less per pupil per year than the national average, because of TABOR. So while it is always important to be a careful steward of the public’s financial resources, we cannot cut our way out of these budget shortfalls, we need to be able to raise revenue. We also need to look at other avenues to increase the state’s finances as we work to repeal TABOR, including closing tax loopholes, and making the wealthiest individuals and corporations pay their fair share for supporting the state and its residents.

What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers?
CAMACHO: Data centers are coming to Colorado, and we need to pass strong regulations and requirements now to ensure we are prepared for their growing prevalence in our state. We don’t want to see a situation like the one our neighbors in Utah are experiencing, and the General Assembly plays an essential role in ensuring that our communities and environment don’t pay the bill for data centers. Additionally, I firmly believe that the state shouldn’t provide financial incentives or tax breaks to data centers, especially while we are fighting to save critical services in the budget. We can expect the conversation around data centers to be a near-permanent fixture in Colorado politics for the foreseeable future. Still, it is clear to me that my constituents are united in opposing handouts and loose regulations for data centers.
HALPERN: I agree with an indefinite moratorium on building new data centers in the state until, and only if, all of our concerns regarding the technology’s development are met. Those concerns are not just limited to the harmful environmental impacts of data centers on air, water, energy consumption, and local utility rates, although those are significant considerations. I am also concerned that a lack of regulation for this industry means we have no assurance that artificial intelligence will be developed with the greater good of our communities in mind. AI development and deployment should promote the interests of ordinary people, not just increase the record wealth inequality we are witnessing. We need to ensure that AI develops so that it does not threaten our communities’ economic health, does not violate our civil and constitutional rights, protects our privacy expectations, reduces the commodification of our data, does not make war more likely or destructive, and keeps our children safe.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy?
CAMACHO: Good policy is not contingent on party affiliation, and I have run some very impactful bills with my colleagues across the aisle as well as members within my party. I believe that if we reject an idea simply because its proponent is not in our party, we could miss many promising opportunities to address our state’s most urgent needs. While I strongly disagree with members of the opposite party on numerous issues, I will not hesitate to work with them when we align on an idea. We must always prioritize good policy and progress, and that is a legislative approach I will continue to employ as long as I am in office. This same philosophy applies to working with members of my own party and is essential to effective policymaking.
HALPERN: Legislation won’t pass and policies won’t advance without working across the aisle and/or within one’s own party. I would do so wherever feasible. Elected officials come from different areas across the state, possess different technical expertise, and can bring different ideas and solutions to the table. We can all learn from each other in that sense. I think it’s important to listen to, learn from and consider those who have had different experiences and serve different constituents with unique problems and needs. However, I also think gaining agreement cannot be an excuse for compromising fundamental values and objectives. Advancing a policy proposal or bill so compromised that it no longer achieves its original objectives, in the name of bipartisanship or uniform party support, gives regulations and laws a veneer of legitimacy that only exacerbates the harm these laws cause to our communities when they are put in place.
As an incumbent, what is one bill, vote or other legislative action you’ve taken that you feel best demonstrates your qualification for reelection?
CAMACHO: One of my proudest accomplishments in the Legislature was passing House Bill 25-1105, or my bill to provide every DPS teacher and staff member with a $2,500 raise for five years without raising taxes. In our current budget crisis, it seemed impossible to increase teacher pay, which our educators desperately need. I demonstrated the creative fiscal problem-solving and out-of-the-box thinking we expect from our elected officials to create real, positive change that our communities can see and feel.
As a challenger, are there any votes the incumbent has taken in the Legislature you disagree with? What are they and why would you have voted differently?
HALPERN: One vote I disagree with is his decision to side with Republicans and vote to kill House Bill 26-1036. This bill would have allowed our mountain communities, at their discretion, to impose a small tax on vacation homes that sit vacant for extensive periods to fund local affordable housing efforts. I also would have voted to amend HB26-1110, Vulnerable Adult Financial Exploitation Banking, to make financial institutions liable for elder fraud transactions if the institution “knew or should have known” the fraud was taking place, which the incumbent opposed. He instead voted in favor of an “actual knowledge” standard which greatly reduced the protection for our elderly community, who are frequently the targets of fraudulent financial schemes. There are a number of other votes he has taken that I disagree with and would have voted differently.
House District 9
 



Monica VanBuskirk
Age: 45
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: VP of Partnerships for Stroke Onward
 


 


Neal Walia
Age: 38
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: Founder and Principal of Lotus Public Affairs LLC
 


Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district?
VANBUSKIRK: Easy! Infinity Park in Glendale. The stadium is one of the premier rugby venues in the country and one of the best-kept secrets in Denver sports. What I love about it is that it works for everyone: Seniors can catch a great match, have a drink, and actually hear each other talk. Families with little kids can get their faces painted and let them run around on the hill. Younger adults can meet new people and learn a new sport. The energy is genuinely fun and community-rooted in a way that bigger venues rarely are. It is also a great entry point into women’s rugby, which has been a big part of my life, including when I won a national championship playing for Glendale. I’m at every home game, and I’m always pulling visitors to watch with us. So come check out a game, I’ll save you a seat. 
WALIA: House District 9 is home to some of my favorite local and historic institutions. I’d take them to The Bagel Deli & Restaurant, Kokoro, Sojourners Coffee & Tea, and Inga’s Alpine Tavern.
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address them? 
VANBUSKIRK: My partner and I both grew up moving around, her family in the military, mine in the migrant stream, so we wanted to raise our kids in one place to down roots. Over the past decade I’ve volunteered at schools and park cleanups, hosted block parties, helped seniors, and knocked on doors to ask what matters to you. Neighbors have told me three things: feeling unsafe, the cost of living, and struggling local businesses. These are connected. A family afraid of ICE doesn’t go out to the corner shop. A senior watching the water bill climb stops tending their yard where neighbors chat. On safety, I would create clear state protections against ICE in schools and workplaces, safer traffic, and invest in what makes a neighborhood feel like a neighborhood again. On cost, I support childcare infrastructure, utility cost controls, and first-time homebuyer help. And I’ve spent 20 years reducing costs for patients, so I know how to make meaningful change in healthcare. As a small business owner, I know the barriers to growth and how both our economy and our environment can thrive. These aren’t issues on a poll, these are what you’ve told me at the front door.
WALIA: The concerns I hear most often center on affordability: the rising cost of healthcare, housing, education, and public safety challenges. My vision begins with healthcare. I support building a universal, single-payer healthcare system and, in the near term, guaranteeing every Coloradan access to a state-funded annual primary care visit. Preventive care lowers costs, improves outcomes, and keeps people healthier. We must also fully fund public education so teachers can afford to live in the communities they serve, retire with dignity, and ensure students have the resources and support they need to thrive. To address housing affordability, I support investments that help first-time homebuyers and working families achieve homeownership. I am particularly interested in exploring innovative approaches, including a graduated mortgage interest-rate pilot program tied to affordable housing development. Public safety requires a balanced approach. We must ensure our communities have the law enforcement personnel they need while also addressing root causes through housing stability, mental health services, substance-use treatment, and economic opportunity. Safe communities are built through both accountability and investment.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation? 
VANBUSKIRK: I’ll answer this honestly instead of just pretend scenarios. There are some places to find efficiency. State service contracts deserve regular review so we know we’re getting what we pay for. Healthcare administration wastes money on paperwork and duplication that does not help patients, and cutting that is good policy and good budgeting at once. But the more powerful answer is on the revenue side, and I’ve done this work. In Trump’s first term, he gave money back to health insurance companies. That sounds bad, but it created an opening. I helped design the mechanism that brought that money back to Colorado and put it straight into lowering healthcare costs for families. That’s the kind of creative, persistent work that actually moves the budget. I’d also change how TABOR artificially limits our budget below inflation. Imagine your family’s income not keeping up with gas prices. That’s not hard to picture, and that’s what TABOR does to the state. It’s a big reason we face the same hard budget choices every year. States that cut their way through tight years without protecting core investments don’t come out stronger. They come out behind.
WALIA: Colorado’s long-term budget challenges cannot be solved through cuts alone. We must have an honest conversation about whether our current revenue system provides sufficient resources to meet the needs of a growing state. I support the graduated income tax ballot measure and strongly support the ballot measure that would allow Colorado to retain and invest additional revenue in public education rather than issuing TABOR refunds. Investing in education is one of the most important things we can do to strengthen our economy, workforce, and future. I also support fully repealing TABOR and replacing it with a more equitable fiscal framework that gives Colorado flexibility to invest in public education, healthcare, housing, transportation, and other priorities while maintaining accountability to taxpayers. As we work toward that goal, we should pursue reforms that allow the state to make the investments our communities need today. I believe large corporations, private equity firms, hedge funds, and the wealthiest individuals should contribute more toward the public services and infrastructure that make our economy possible. We should explore targeted fees, taxes, and accountability measures that ensure powerful economic actors pay their fair share and do not extract profits at the expense of Colorado families and communities.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers? 
VANBUSKIRK: Denver City Council’s unanimous vote to pause data center development was the right call. We’re in a severe drought. If you asked me what to build for Colorado’s economy, the last thing I’d pick is a building that drinks this much water. Regional water use for data centers could balloon to over 89,700 acre-feet by 2035, even as we pay millions of dollars on projects for farmers to conserve water. Why save water on food and then hand it to data centers? We also have wild inflation. The last thing I’d choose is a corporate giveaway that raises Coloradans’ electric bills to subsidize an industry. Look at Virginia, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world. Tax breaks there cost the state $1 billion annually, and the centers pay less than standard utility rates. I won’t accept a status quo where communities near these sites carry the environmental burden while the industry keeps the profit. We need smarter approaches that protect our water and wildlife, lower utility costs for residents, create lasting jobs, and keep our state healthy for future generations.
WALIA: Colorado should proceed thoughtfully and responsibly regarding data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure. I support a temporary pause on new large-scale data center development while we study the economic, environmental, public health, energy, and water-use impacts on our communities. If Colorado moves forward with expanding data center development, these facilities must be strongly regulated to meet the highest standards for energy efficiency, water conservation, environmental stewardship, transparency, and data privacy. Economic development cannot come at the expense of our natural resources, public health, or consumer protections.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy? 
VANBUSKIRK: Most of my career has meant working through division, and I’m good at it. I’m a mom, so I negotiate at every meal. As the former chief policy officer at Connect for Health, every bill I worked on was bipartisan. I spent years on a cost task force beside a Republican I disagreed with, but it worked because we cared about facts and didn’t make it personal. But bipartisan work doesn’t mean conceding every time. One of my boundaries is when something causes harm. I don’t tolerate it at home or at work. Within my Democratic party, we should be honest about tradeoffs instead of pretending we can fund everything at once. This honors our voters and is why I have so many state legislators’ endorsements. I’ve filled out citizenship paperwork, seen votes on my marriage, and am the only parent in this race. But I’m also the only one who has successfully written and passed multiple Colorado bills: easier tax credits for families; zero-dollar mental health visits for nearly 140,000 people; hundreds of millions in health insurance help for working families. That’s receipts over rhetoric. 
WALIA: Throughout my career, I have worked successfully with diverse coalitions across the political spectrum. As director of government relations and policy for the Colorado Academy of Family Physicians, I helped advance legislation to eliminate non-compete agreements in healthcare. At the Asian Pacific Development Center, I worked alongside legislators and community organizations from different backgrounds to help establish Lunar New Year as an official Colorado state holiday. I believe effective governing requires strong principles, meaningful stakeholder engagement, and a willingness to find common ground where it exists. While there will always be issues on which people disagree, I focus on solutions rather than political division. My goal is to build coalitions around practical policies that improve people’s lives and strengthen our communities.
House District 13
 


Chris Floyd
Age: Not available
City of residence: Leadville
Occupation: Attorney
 


 



Consuelo Redhorse
Age: 47
City of residence: Silverthorne
Occupation: Bookkeeper
 


Floyd did not return a questionnaire.
Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district?
REDHORSE: House District 13 is the most beautiful district in Colorado and has so much to offer. A thorough visit could easily take a month, with different activities, sights to see, and communities to visit. However, if I had only one day to share with an out-of-town friend, I would highlight Summit County, my home of 15 years and the place that has shaped my life and inspired me to run for office. My friend and I would start our day on Frisco Main Street, supporting local businesses and neighbors who are the heart of our communities. We would hike in the White River National Forest, just steps away from my front door, enjoying the serene, natural beauty offered within our public lands. We would finish the day with a show at the beautiful Dillon Amphitheater, a venue that connects locals and visitors through their love of music. Throughout this visit, we would certainly run into friends and community members from all walks of life. These experiences would encourage a deep appreciation of experiences, places, and viewpoints that represent just a small slice of House District 13.
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
REDHORSE: Each of our communities experiences its own unique challenges, however consistent themes include cost of living, access to services, community safety, and protecting public lands. Community members I have spoken with are concerned about the lack of housing that meets their needs, access to healthcare and childcare, wildfires and drought, feeling safe in their own communities, public education funding, and persistent increases in cost of gas, groceries, and basic utilities. Addressing these issues must be done in partnership with communities throughout House District 13, and requires listening to understand their life experiences, how policies are affecting them, and high-impact solutions that will work for our communities. As your representative, I will listen to understand and make decisions with you, not for you. I will fight for sustainable programs and policies that support healthy, safe communities and make sense in mountain and rural areas. I will fight for a fair tax system that does not bind Colorado to outdated, inflexible, and arbitrary caps. I will clearly communicate the lived experiences and needs within our mountain and rural communities to ensure that our voices are heard in a system that tends to highlight the needs of the Front Range.

My focus will always be on what is best for Pueblo County.
Senate District 21
 



Adrienne Benavidez (incumbent)
Age: Not available
City of residence: Commerce City
Occupation: State senator
 


 



Alex Ryckman

Age: 35
City of residence: Unincorporated Adams County
Occupation: Teacher
 


Benavidez did not return a questionnaire.
Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district?
RYCKMAN: I know this is very food centered but breakfast at Mr. Egg or Tasty Donuts, lunch at Paisano’s, afternoon coffee at Subjective Coffee and dinner at Las Delicias. Or we could just go all in and spend the day at the Mile High Flea Market eating elotes, browsing antiques and doing the big slide! This district has amazing food and awesome things to do. I love my community and am truly that person that will drive you all around to show you old spaces, take you to good food and highlight what makes us special.
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it?
RYCKMAN: I think that affordability is the biggest issue that I hear about from my community. I typically respond by bringing up how privatization is to blame for a lot of our rising costs and problems. I want to address this by increasing protections for workers, especially when so many people live paycheck to paycheck. Affordability would be less of a problem if we all were paid a fair wage and were respected for the work that we do. I also want to fully fund schools so we aren’t constantly putting pressure on small businesses and property taxes through mill levies to supplement where the state is not able to fund us. Finally, I think that we need to invest in Colorado and keep our tax dollars in our state by supporting local businesses and universities rather than supporting private companies and outside interests to “fix” things we can handle on our own.
This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation?
RYCKMAN: I would be interested to know how anyone would reduce spending when we’ve cut at least $1 billion from the budget every year for the past two years. I don’t know how much longer we can sustain such a deficit every year. The people of Colorado have deemed which programming is most important and we need to honor them and fund schools, healthcare, and sustainable options. I think we need to first address TABOR and how it limits funding. We also need to elect officials that we trust to spend our money wisely without special interests. But until then, we need to sharpen our magnifying glass on privatization and organizations that are taking advantage of taxpayer money.
What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers?
RYCKMAN: I think that if we want to truly be proactive instead of reactive, we need to invest in education around the dangers and the necessity of data centers. With the constant discussion of the cloud, it is easy to think of data as not needing a physical home, but centers to store our information are not going away. Police body cameras are a great example of a policy that I strongly support that also comes with a massive amount of data that has to be stored on servers somewhere. When it comes to AI data centers, that is a different conversation. That does not mean that I think the areas of my district that continue to be taken advantage of should get flooded with new AI data centers and that our water and energy should just pour into these facilities. We need to look at policies that regulate the use of AI and its impact on our communities and our world, more than just thinking that by stopping data centers in our community, we are stopping the problem.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy?
RYCKMAN: We get places by doing work together. I am a teacher. If I just had my own worldview and didn’t listen to others or seek to understand, then I would not still be in my profession. We have to start working together to find common ground and shared values. I am adamantly against the two items on our ballot in November attacking trans children. For me, that is because I believe in trans rights and support their right to be who they are. I think all children should be allowed to be themselves and their guardians should be able to walk alongside them and support them in their journey. I believe that the government has no business checking my daughter’s gender and many of my friends, colleagues, and constituents, no matter their affiliation, share this view. My job in the state Senate is to represent all of District 21, and that means I don’t get to just listen to folks who believe the same things that I do. I will seek to understand rather than be understood in this office, and when we do disagree I promise to take the time to explain the why behind my choice.
Are there any votes the incumbent has taken in the Legislature you disagree with? What are they and why would you have voted differently?
RYCKMAN: I disagree with the incumbent’s legislation around school board qualifications, Senate Bill 26-166. The proposed bill would prohibit people from serving on a school board based on certain drug charges and time since conviction. Voters should have the ability to decide who they believe is best suited to represent them. If someone does not feel a candidate is qualified or fit to serve, they have the power to make that decision at the ballot box. We have a justice system that’s supposed to be centered on rehabilitation, and I cannot stand by policy that further stigmatizes people who have already been penalized and are looking to give back to their community. I will also name that my largest disappointment with my opponent has been the lack of communication about the legislative session. Communication and engagement with constituents throughout the session has been limited. I have seen very few opportunities for community input through town halls, public updates, or updates at the end of session. Representation should involve listening, communicating openly, and keeping constituents informed, and that is something I would prioritize as your representative.
 Senate District 34
 



Chela Garcia Irlando
Age: 34
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: Environmental nonprofit executive director
 


 


Andrés Carrera
Age: 33
City of residence: Denver
Occupation: Nonprofit director
 


Where would you take an out-of-town friend to visit in your district? 
GARCIA IRLANDO: There are too many amazing options for one! We could spend several days in Senate District 34. First, we’d grab a coffee at Convivio and take a walk around Sloan’s Lake. Since we’d have our kids with us, we’d have to stop at the rocketship playground at Sloan’s. Then, we could hop across Federal Boulevard to visit Meow Wolf to escape the heat and enjoy amazing interactive and sensory art. For lunch, we’d grab a banh mi sandwich and boba from New Saigon Bakery and Deli, then we’d hop on our bikes, take the Weir Gulch Trail to the South Platte River Trail and head towards downtown. We’d stop by Elitch’s to cool off in their water park and get on some thrilling rides. Then, we’d end the night watching a Rockies game or hanging out at Inspiration Point, the best sunset in the city.
CARRERA: First, I would take them to eat some of the best tacos at El Taco de Mexico, the James Beard award-winning, all-woman taqueria located off Santa Fe and 7th Avenue, and I would time the visit around First Friday so we could see all of the incredible art exhibits on display in the area afterward. First Friday is my all-time favorite Denver tradition. But no trip to West Denver would be complete without a visit to Sloan’s Lake, or the adjacent Odell Brewhouse, so we’d have to check that off our list, too. On Sunday, we’d go up to the Highlands Square Farmers Market off Lowell Boulevard and 32nd Avenue and buy coffee from Café Zuri owners Tomas and Mariana, who also have some of the best Czech pastries you’ll ever try. We’d finish it off with a visit to Larimer Square (can’t leave out the most Instagrammable spot in town), Union Station, and Coors Field or Empower Field at Mile High, depending on whether the Rockies or the Broncos are in season.
What do residents in your district say are the community’s biggest issues, and how will you work to address it? 
GARCIA IRLANDO: Affordability, first and foremost. The extremely high cost of living continues to outpace wages, forcing families to make difficult financial choices, take on lifelong debt, and face displacement away from the communities they love and are rooted in. I support rent stabilization for both residents and small businesses alike, building more multifamily housing that is actually affordable for people, bans on corporate ownership of single-family homes, and prohibiting algorithmic rent pricing. I plan to expand protections for workers to ensure better wages and working conditions because our workforce drives our local economy. Check out ChelaForColorado.Com for more information on how I plan to address affordability and inequality, both in my district and across Colorado.
CARRERA: When I’m knocking on doors and speaking with residents, they all say the same thing: costs are high, wages are low, and so is their tolerance of a hostile White House that seems focused on terrorizing our communities with ICE raids rather than solving actual problems. As a son of immigrants who grew up watching his grandparents work as janitors, farmworkers, and seamstresses, that hits close to home. That’s why I’m proposing free childcare, a guaranteed path to homeownership for all college and trade school graduates, and nonprofit grocery stores to slash the cost of living in concrete ways the average family can feel month after month. It’s possible. And after getting $7.5 million in federal funding for our community, helping 5,500 immigrants connect with work permits, being part of the team that housed 1,000 people experiencing homelessness in Denver, and helping 500,000 Coloradans survive the COVID-19 pandemic, I have the experience to turn those ideas into reality.

This was the second year in a row the Legislature had to make deep program cuts to balance the state budget. Where can the state reduce its spending, and what is your view on how Colorado can return to a positive budget situation? 
GARCIA IRLANDO: I’m carrying petitions for the graduated income tax when I’m going door to door, and people are incredibly supportive. Millionaires and large corporations can afford to pay their fair share to benefit all Coloradans, especially since our state provides public infrastructure — such as roads, education, and utility infrastructure — that corporations depend on. I support the recent bill passed by the Legislature to refer a ballot measure to the 2026 general election to increase public K-12 education funding by up to 2% per year for 10 years. There was also a recent attempt by the state Legislature to collect a fee on large corporations, with over 500 employees, for any workers dependent on public assistance benefits, with an exception for workers eligible for assistance benefits based on disability. I fully support this approach because I believe that tax payers should not be subsidizing benefits for large corporations that can afford to pay for their workers’ benefits, but refuse to do so. Lastly, I believe that we must cut Colorado’s $1 billion plus spending on private prisons by reducing our non-violent offender prison population, and redirect that funding towards community-based prevention, education, mental health and healthcare, and the social safety net.
CARRERA: I’ll tell you where the state can’t reduce its spending. We must protect programs that mean the difference between life and death for Coloradans. Funding for Medicaid, for example, is non-negotiable. Funding for food, nutritional, behavioral health, and suicide crisis services must also be protected. We all know how cold Colorado winters can get, so I would also defend funding for Low-income Energy Assistance Programs (LEAP) which helps families pay a portion of their winter home heating costs. All other programs in the state budget must be seriously scrutinized line-by-line and evaluated based on whether data shows they are effective uses of taxpayer dollars.

What policies should the state enact regarding the proliferation of data centers? 
GARCIA IRLANDO: I support strict regulations on data centers to protect communities, our water and our climate. For decades the oil and gas industry has polluted our communities and natural resources while the state Legislature and utilities have provided incentives and regulatory exemptions to this industry. I strongly oppose the same playbook proposed by data centers that would bind our state in deficit contracts, leave accountability to the will of corporations, and bypass any safeguards against polluting our communities. I support data center accountability policies such as public health and cumulative impact safeguards, strict water use and conservation parameters, renewable energy requirements, and mandates to ensure any new public utility infrastructure built to provide service to data centers is fully paid for by data center developers and not taxpayers or utility ratepayers. I also support enacting these policies with enforceable oversight mechanisms to ensure data center corporations do not treat noncompliance as the cost of doing business. Given these proposed parameters and accountability measures, I support a moratorium on data centers to guarantee protections for communities, public health, and our water and climate.
CARRERA: Data centers use about as much water as a small town. And considering the rest of Denver can’t even water its lawn right now, it’s not the right time to allow a gargantuan building to guzzle what little water we have. Estimates also show that data centers are expected to account for 12% of all U.S. energy consumption by 2028. Unless they’re able to run on renewable energy and not increase energy costs for residents, I’m a “no” on allowing them to come into our communities.
What is your view on working across the aisle, and within your own party, to advance policy? 
GARCIA IRLANDO: I will work with anyone who wants to work to improve the lives of working people, protect the environment, create universal healthcare and childcare, and make Colorado more affordable for all of us, regardless of party. I will not compromise my values, regardless of party. As someone who has spent my career as a community organizer, nonprofit leader, and working collaboratively in coalitions across Colorado and nationally, I strongly believe that policy should not be decided in silos, but rather built in direct partnership with the people who are most impacted by those decisions. I was recently endorsed by Senator Bernie Sanders, an unaffiliated elected official, who understands that injustice is not a partisan issue, thus the solutions must also be grounded in the impacts to real people and not partisanship. I am excited to carry this approach to the Colorado Legislature, to work collaboratively but also fight when needed, to get things done.
CARRERA: Whenever I helped veterans connect with Social Security benefits, I never asked for their party affiliation. Whenever I connected people experiencing homelessness with housing, I never asked who they voted for in the last presidential election. None of that matters. What matters is helping people, and I’ll link arms with anyone who is interested in putting forward solutions to help the 6 million people who call Colorado home, regardless of whether they’re Democrats or Republicans. Ideas can only get sharper by having conversations with people we disagree with – people who have vastly different life experiences from my own. And that’s what I plan to do as state senator.

title: Alabama Attorney General threatens legal action against six abortion pill providers
description: The Alabama Attorney General’s Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies that it said were advertising or distributing abortion-inducing medication to Alabamians. “Alabama’s law is clear, abortion is illegal in this state. These companies are not only breaking the law, they are deceiving Alabama consumers about the very real dangers of[...]
text:
Mifepristone is one of two drugs that can be used before 10 weeks to terminate a pregnancy and to treat miscarriages. The Alabama Attorney General's Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies that distribute the medication to consumers in the state that has a near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) 


Key points

The Alabama Attorney General’s Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies it said were advertising or distributing medication to induce abortions, citing Alabama law that makes performing or attempting to perform an abortion a felony.
The office cited a study from a conservative think tank on abortion pill complications that has drawn criticism over its methodology.
A reproductive rights advocate said the letter was “an enormous commercial” for the companies.
The letters were signed by Deputy Attorney General Katherine Robertson, who is competing in next week’s Republican runoff for attorney general and who has been criticized by her opponent, former Alabama Supreme Court Justice Jay Mitchell, for accepting contributions from a man who has criticized Alabama’s near-total abortion ban.




The Alabama Attorney General’s Office on Tuesday threatened legal action against six companies that it said were advertising or distributing abortion-inducing medication to Alabamians.
“Alabama’s law is clear, abortion is illegal in this state. These companies are not only breaking the law, they are deceiving Alabama consumers about the very real dangers of these drugs. That stops now,” Attorney General Steve Marshall said in a statement. “Anyone who tries to exploit Alabamians for profit while flouting our laws will be prosecuted to the fullest extent permitted by law.”
In doing so, the office effectively advertised where Alabamians seeking an abortion can get medication, said Robin Marty, executive director of the West Alabama Women’s Center, which provided abortion care before Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022.
“As a person who is heavily involved in reproductive access for all people, I am surprised that he does not realize that what he has done has essentially provided an enormous commercial for these companies,” Marty said.
